The SUPPORT Act's reauthorization is a critical step, but let's be clear—Washington's track record on opioid crisis spending demands scrutiny. While H.R.2483 allocates $505.6M annually for overdose prevention (Sec.103) and $38.9M for maternal treatment programs (Sec.201), we've seen similar allocations vanish into bureaucratic black holes under previous administrations.

The 51.7% spending surge from FY2019-2024 (DOGE Agency Spending Table) proves money alone doesn't fix systemic failures. This bill must ensure funds actually reach frontline providers, not get absorbed by administrative bloat.

The Trump administration's focus should be enforcing strict accountability measures—like mandatory quarterly expenditure audits and clawback provisions for underperforming grants—to prevent another cycle of wasted taxpayer dollars.

The SUPPORT Act's reauthorization pours $505 million annually into overdose monitoring programs (Section 103) and $38.9M for maternal addiction treatment (Section 201), but where's the accountability? While expanding fentanyl test strip access (Section 113) is smart, H.R. 2483 still funnels millions into bloated bureaucracies like the $100M National Child Traumatic Stress Initiative (Section 107) without performance metrics.

The 366-57 House vote shows bipartisan concern, but real success requires redirecting funds from redundant "technical assistance centers" (Section 302) to frontline clinics.

Taxpayers deserve proof these programs reduce overdoses beyond current 107,000 annual deaths – not just feel-good reauthorizations.
